assessment.nobel_worthiness: Created modern quantitative political economics by embedding electoral rules, constitutions, state capacity and fiscal policy in formal models that are tested empirically. The field changed how economists treat institutions and policy formation, and it is closely tied to the institutions-and-growth research recognised in recent years.
assessment.attribution: The Persson-Tabellini constitutional and electoral-rule programme and the Besley-Persson work on state capacity form a coherent three-person core. Others, such as Acemoglu and Alesina, are already recognised or are outside this list, so the credit is fairly concentrated here.
assessment.maturity: Foundational work dates from the 1990s and 2000s. It has been replicated, extended and used in policy and teaching for 20 to 30 years, which makes it fully mature.
uncertainties: Some proposed laureates may be institutionally close to Stockholm (IIES), which is a disclosed proximity that I do not adjudicate here.
The field is broad, so one could argue that more contributors deserve credit than three.
Overlap with the 2024 institutions prize may make some members regard the area as partly covered.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Established the task-based, skill-biased and trade-exposure accounts of labour-demand change and wage polarisation, with the China-shock evidence showing persistent local effects. The work reshaped both academic and public understanding of technology, globalisation and inequality.
assessment.attribution: The task framework and polarisation evidence are chiefly Autor, Katz and their co-authors, and the trade-shock work is Autor, Dorn and Hanson. Katz's earlier work is a major foundation. Dorn is a real contributor but the three-name limit forces his exclusion. Related work by Goldin, Acemoglu and others overlaps.
assessment.maturity: Core papers date from 1992 to 2013 and have a large citation and policy record. The findings on persistence are well replicated, though the AI-era extensions are still open.
uncertainties: The three-name limit excludes David Dorn.
Partial overlap with the 2023 prize on labour-market outcomes and the 2024 growth work.
Debate continues over the relative roles of technology and trade.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Showed quantitatively that misallocation of inputs across heterogeneous firms can explain a large share of cross-country income and TFP differences. This gave growth and development economics a measurable mechanism and a standard toolkit.
assessment.attribution: Hsieh-Klenow (2009) and Restuccia-Rogerson (2008) are the two simultaneous, foundational contributions. Rogerson is not credited in this list, which weakens the attribution picture. The three listed names are the clearest.
assessment.maturity: The work is 15 to 18 years old with a vast follow-on literature. It has been challenged on measurement but remains standard.
uncertainties: Measurement concerns about whether measured dispersion reflects true misallocation or mismeasurement.
Rogerson's exclusion from the credited names leaves the attribution incomplete.
The prize may be seen as more of a methodological contribution than a discovery.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Nominal rigidities, staggered pricing and wage contracts, and the micro-founded New Keynesian framework with interest-rate rules underpin modern monetary-policy analysis and inflation targeting. This is institutionally central to central banking worldwide.
assessment.attribution: Credit is spread across at least eight names (Calvo, Taylor, Woodford, Gali, Gertler, Christiano, Eichenbaum, Smets). Calvo's pricing, Taylor's contracts and rule, and Woodford's synthesis are the most defensible three. Others, such as Rotemberg, Clarida and Gali, could reasonably be argued for.
assessment.maturity: The framework dates from the 1980s to the early 2000s and has been tested through the inflation targeting era, the financial crisis and the post-pandemic inflation. It is mature, but the recent inflation episode has prompted debate.
uncertainties: Very diffuse attribution makes a three-person selection contestable.
Partial overlap with the 2022 prize and earlier macro prizes (Lucas, Sargent, Sims, Kydland-Prescott).
Post-2021 inflation raises questions about the framework's performance.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Kiyotaki-Moore (1997) formalised the credit cycle, in which collateral constraints and asset prices amplify and propagate shocks. It is the theoretical backbone of much macro-financial modelling, including how research since 2008 treats financial frictions.
assessment.attribution: The Kiyotaki-Moore mechanism is a clear two-person contribution. Bernanke, Gertler and Gilchrist's financial accelerator is a related strand, and Bernanke is already a laureate, so I keep the proposal to Kiyotaki and Moore to avoid diluting attribution.
assessment.maturity: Nearly 30 years of use, extended by many studies of the financial crisis and the macroprudential frameworks that followed. It is fully mature.
uncertainties: Partial overlap with the 2022 prize on banking and financial crises.
Whether the committee prefers to include Gertler and Gilchrist's competing strand.
The empirical identification of the mechanism is indirect.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The heterogeneous-firm framework changed trade theory by explaining selection, exporter premia and the gains from trade through firm-level productivity differences. It became the dominant approach in trade research.
assessment.attribution: Melitz (2003) is the central paper and Helpman's multi-decade contributions (with Krugman, Grossman and others) established the broader framework. Redding is a significant contributor on quantitative and spatial extensions, but less central to the firm-selection discovery. Krugman's 2008 prize partly covers the preceding new trade theory.
assessment.maturity: Over 20 years of work and very widely used, with extensive empirical confirmation.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2008 Krugman prize.
Helpman is also credited in B049, which splits attribution.
Whether the committee sees the framework as a theoretical refinement or a discovery.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Linked optimal taxation theory with empirical elasticities of taxable income, bunching methods and sufficient-statistics approaches. This changed how tax policy is evaluated and informed practical design.
assessment.attribution: Slemrod and Saez drove the taxable-income elasticity agenda, and Chetty developed the sufficient-statistics method. Feldstein, who is deceased, was a precursor. Stantcheva's contributions are newer and she is excluded from this selection. Saez and Chetty also appear in other entries, which could split credit.
assessment.maturity: The early work is 25 years old, but the Chetty and Stantcheva extensions are recent and still being tested.
uncertainties: Overlap with other entries naming Saez and Chetty.
Identification of elasticities from bunching is contested.
Part of the field is still young, so recent contributions are not fully confirmed.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Formal models of present bias, self-control problems and reference dependence brought psychologically realistic preferences into mainstream theory and applied work on savings, contracts and consumption. Their influence is broad across fields.
assessment.attribution: Laibson (quasi-hyperbolic discounting), Rabin (psychology-informed theory) and Koszegi (with Rabin, reference-dependent preferences) are a plausible trio. O'Donoghue and Loewenstein have substantial claims and Kahneman and Thaler already covered the behavioural foundations.
assessment.maturity: The work spans 1990s to 2000s, with mixed but extensive empirical support across applications.
uncertainties: Partial overlap with the 2002 Kahneman and 2017 Thaler prizes.
Mixed field evidence for reference dependence and for present bias.
Several equally plausible alternative combinations of names.
